headline: Training covered New Hampshire collective bargaining law as the district negotiates with six employee groups.
summary: Attorney Matthew Upton explained how bargaining subjects are sorted into mandatory, permissive, and prohibited categories. He also described the steps for approving a tentative agreement, including ratification and municipal approval of cost items. Specific negotiating strategies were set aside for a separate discussion after the public meeting.

BOARD OF SCHOOL COMMITTEE 
SPECIAL MEETING – BOARD TRAINING 
MANCHESTER SCHOOL DISTRICT SAU #37 
 
October 28, 2026 6:00 p.m.  
 
1. Mayor Ruais called the meeting to order at 6:00 p.m. 
 
Mayor Jay Ruais called the October 28, 2026, special meeting of the Board of School Committee to 
order. He noted that the meeting was scheduled to adjourn by 8:00 p.m., although that time was not a 
mandatory adjournment deadline. 
 
2. Mayor Ruais called for the Pledge of Allegiance. 
 
3. The Clerk called the roll.  
 
Present:  Committee Members Turner, Want, Taylor, O’Connell (6:07 p.m.), 
Spencer, St. John, Garrity, O’Neil-Wong (6:03), Smith, and Mayor Ruais. 
 
Absent: Committee Members Parr, Georges, Stewart, and Hamerwere absent.  
Ward 6 seat still vacant at this time. 
 
PUBLIC FORUM 
 
There was no one present wishing to give public comment. 
 
5.   Collective Bargaining – by Matthew H. Upton, Executive Director of Legal and Policy 
 
 
Attorney Matthew Upton provided training to the Board regarding New Hampshire's collective 
bargaining laws, the responsibilities of public employers, negotiation procedures, and the approval of 
collective bargaining agreements. 
 
Attorney Upton explained that the Manchester School District was currently engaged in negotiations 
with its bargaining units. The purpose of the training was to provide Board members with an 
understanding of the legal requirements governing negotiations and their responsibilities as the public 
employer. 
 
He indicated that the presentation would focus on general collective bargaining laws and procedures. 
Discussions regarding specific negotiating strategies or current contract proposals would be reserved 
for a separate discussion following the public meeting.
October 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 2 of 13 
 
New Hampshire Public Employee Labor Relations Act 
Attorney Upton explained that the New Hampshire Public Employee Labor Relations Act was 
adopted in 1975 as public employees throughout the country increasingly organized and sought 
collective bargaining rights.  He stated that the central purpose of the law is to require public 
employers to negotiate in good faith with the exclusive representatives of certified bargaining units 
regarding terms and conditions of employment. 
 
Attorney Upton emphasized that not every matter affecting school operations is subject to collective 
bargaining. He explained that bargaining subjects fall into three categories: 
 Mandatory subjects: Matters the District is legally required to negotiate. 
 Permissive subjects: Matters the District may voluntarily negotiate but is not required to 
negotiate. 
 Prohibited subjects: Matters that cannot be negotiated because they fall within the District's 
statutory or managerial authority. 
 
The bargaining process may result in a tentative agreement, which must be ratified by the appropriate 
parties before becoming an approved collective bargaining agreement. 
 
Exclusive Representation and Bargaining Unit Certification 
 
Attorney Upton explained that collective bargaining units must be certified by the New Hampshire 
Public Employee Labor Relations Board (PELRB).  The certification process determines which 
positions are included in a bargaining unit and identifies the exclusive representative authorized to 
negotiate on behalf of those employees. 
 
He emphasized the following: 
 The District must negotiate with the certified bargaining representative rather than individual 
employees. 
 Negotiating directly with employees regarding mandatory subjects of bargaining is 
considered direct dealing and may constitute an unfair labor practice. 
 Certain positions may be excluded from collective bargaining representation, including 
elected officials, certain School Board appointees, employees with confidential labor relations 
responsibilities, and certain temporary or probationary employees.
October 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 3 of 13 
 
 Bargaining unit certifications and collective bargaining agreements are available for public 
review through the PELRB website. 
 
Attorney Upton explained that New Hampshire law generally requires at least ten public employees 
with a community of interest to establish a bargaining unit.  A community of interest is determined 
by considering factors such as working conditions, schedules, employment responsibilities, and job 
duties. He referenced a legal case involving police and fire personnel attempting to form a combined 
bargaining unit and explained how differences in their duties and schedules affected the 
determination of whether a sufficient community of interest existed. 
 
Managerial Prerogatives 
 
Attorney Upton explained that certain decisions remain within the District's managerial authority and 
are not required subjects of collective bargaining.  These decisions generally include the selection 
and direction of personnel, the number of employees, legitimate departmental reorganizations, and 
the elimination of positions resulting from restructuring.  He emphasized that the Board must retain 
the authority necessary to manage school operations and fulfill its educational responsibilities. 
 
Good Faith Bargaining 
 
Attorney Upton explained that New Hampshire law requires the parties to participate in good faith 
negotiations.  He emphasized that the obligation to bargain in good faith does not require either party 
to agree to a particular proposal.  Both parties must be willing to discuss proposals and participate 
meaningfully in the negotiating process. However, a party may reject a proposal without violating the 
law.  Attorney Upton also explained that either party may declare an impasse and request mediation 
when an agreement cannot be reached. 
 
Mandatory Subjects of Bargaining 
 
Attorney Upton reviewed mandatory bargaining subjects, which generally involve wages, hours, and 
terms and conditions of employment. 
Examples included: 
 Wages and salary schedules.
October 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 4 of 13 
 
 Length of the workday. 
 Health insurance benefits. 
 Vacation schedules. 
 Grievance procedures. 
 Union rights. 
 Contract duration. 
He noted that collective bargaining agreements must contain workable grievance procedures. 
 
Permissive Subjects of Bargaining 
 
Attorney Upton explained that permissive subjects are matters the District is not legally required to 
negotiate but may voluntarily include in a collective bargaining agreement.  Examples discussed 
included just-cause disciplinary standards, layoff and recall procedures, reassignment, involuntary 
transfers, bell schedules, and employee evaluation procedures.  Attorney Upton discussed several 
examples specific to Manchester: 
 Just cause: Many established agreements include just-cause provisions establishing standards 
for determining whether disciplinary action is appropriate and fair. 
 Involuntary transfers: The Manchester Education Association (MEA) agreement establishes 
procedures that must be followed when employees are involuntarily transferred. When those 
procedures are satisfied, the decision may not be subject to grievance or arbitration. 
 Bell schedules: The existing MEA agreement includes provisions regarding school bell 
schedules. Because those provisions were previously negotiated into the agreement, changes 
now require negotiations with the union. 
 Evaluations: Certain employee evaluation procedures may be addressed through collective 
bargaining, and the District was reviewing related provisions. 
 
Attorney Upton emphasized that including permissive subjects in an agreement may limit the 
District's future operational flexibility. He explained that the bell schedule is a current example of a 
matter that might otherwise have remained within managerial discretion but now requires negotiation 
because of its inclusion in the collective bargaining agreement.
October 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 5 of 13 
 
Prohibited Subjects of Bargaining 
 
Attorney Upton reviewed matters that remain within the District's educational and statutory authority. 
Examples included job classifications and duties, promotion criteria, class sizes, curriculum, student 
discipline requirements, and graduation criteria.  He explained that the District must retain the 
authority necessary to respond to changes in student enrollment and educational needs. 
Attorney Upton also discussed student discipline, particularly as it relates to students with 
disabilities.  He noted that students may have individualized behavioral intervention plans or other 
legally required supports established through the special education process. Collective bargaining 
agreements cannot override federal special education requirements or the authority of an 
Individualized Education Program (IEP) team. 
 
Collective Bargaining Agreement Approval Process 
 
Attorney Upton reviewed the steps required for a tentative agreement to become an approved 
collective bargaining agreement.  He explained that a tentative agreement must be ratified by the 
bargaining unit membership and approved by the Board of School Committee. 
In addition, any cost items requiring appropriations must receive approval from the Board of Mayor 
and Aldermen.  Attorney Upton emphasized that the Board of Mayor and Aldermen's statutory 
approval authority is limited to cost items.  He explained that although aldermen may express 
concerns regarding other contractual provisions, their formal role is to approve the financial 
obligations associated with an agreement. 
 
Cost Items 
 
Attorney Upton explained that cost items are benefits negotiated through collective bargaining that 
require an appropriation.  Examples include: 
 Wages and salary increases. 
 Stipends. 
 Health, dental, and life insurance. 
 Retirement-related benefits. 
 Severance obligations.
October 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 6 of 13 
 
He emphasized that these financial commitments must receive the necessary municipal approval 
before implementation. 
 
Impasse and Dispute Resolution 
 
Mediation 
Attorney Upton explained that either party may request mediation when negotiations reach an 
impasse. Mediation is a nonbinding process in which an independent mediator works with both 
parties to identify possible solutions to outstanding issues. 
 
He emphasized that mediation discussions are confidential. Proposals, statements, and discussions 
occurring during mediation generally cannot be disclosed publicly or used in subsequent fact-finding 
proceedings.  Although the parties may acknowledge that mediation occurred and that an agreement 
was not reached, they must respect the confidentiality of the discussions. 
 
Negotiation Ground Rules 
Attorney Upton explained that bargaining teams typically establish ground rules before negotiations 
begin.  These rules outline expectations regarding: 
 The format and submission of proposals. 
 How proposed contract changes are identified. 
 Documentation of tentative agreements. 
 Confidentiality during negotiations. 
 Communication between representatives and their respective members or governing bodies. 
Attorney Upton stated that he prefers proposals to contain specific contract language, using 
strikethroughs for proposed deletions and bold text for additions.  He explained that tentative 
agreements are generally reduced to writing and initialed by the parties as negotiations progress. 
This process allows both sides to maintain an accurate record and reduces the potential for 
misunderstandings. 
 
Confidentiality During Negotiations 
Attorney Upton explained that bargaining ground rules typically require negotiations to remain 
confidential.  Union representatives may communicate with their membership, while District 
representatives may provide updates to the Board of School Committee.
October 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 7 of 13 
 
 
He cautioned that tentative agreements on individual issues can change as negotiations continue. 
For example, an agreement involving health insurance benefits may later be reconsidered in 
exchange for a different salary proposal. 
 
Attorney Upton explained that prematurely announcing tentative provisions as final could create 
confusion and dissatisfaction during the ratification process.  He also noted that, following a 
declaration of impasse, the parties may have greater latitude to discuss their negotiating positions 
publicly.  However, he discouraged public criticism or adversarial statements that could increase 
tension and make mediation more difficult.  He recommended maintaining professional and 
constructive communications throughout the process. 
 
Fact-Finding 
Attorney Upton explained that New Hampshire utilizes an advisory fact-finding process when 
negotiations remain unresolved following mediation.  He contrasted this process with states that 
utilize binding interest arbitration.  In New Hampshire, fact-finding recommendations are not 
automatically binding upon the parties.  The recommendations generally require acceptance by the 
applicable parties, with financial commitments remaining subject to the necessary funding approvals. 
Attorney Upton explained that fact-finding can still be beneficial because a neutral recommendation 
may encourage either party to reconsider its position. 
 
He noted that a willingness by the Board of Mayor and Aldermen to fund a recommendation could 
also influence whether the parties are willing to accept it. 
Unfair Labor Practices and Negotiating Conduct 
 
Attorney Upton reviewed actions that public employers and bargaining representatives should avoid 
during negotiations. 
 
These included: 
 Direct dealing: Negotiating directly with employees instead of their certified bargaining 
representative. 
 Coercion: Attempting to pressure employees into accepting proposals through threats or 
inappropriate conduct.
October 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 8 of 13 
 
 Retaliation: Taking adverse action against employees because of positions expressed during 
negotiations. 
 Surface bargaining: Participating in negotiations without a genuine intention of attempting 
to reach an agreement. 
 Regressive bargaining: Reducing or withdrawing a previously offered benefit as a means of 
pressuring the other party. 
 Negotiating without intent to support an agreement: Agreeing to provisions with the 
expectation that the Board of Mayor and Aldermen will subsequently reject the associated 
financial commitments. 
 
Attorney Upton explained that parties may mutually agree to reconsider proposals as part of broader 
negotiations.  For example, a salary proposal may be adjusted when the parties agree to consider 
different health insurance provisions.  He emphasized that these changes should result from 
legitimate negotiations rather than punitive or coercive bargaining tactics. 
 
Attorney Upton also discussed the importance of professional conduct, noting that personal attacks, 
aggressive behavior, and intentionally misleading statements can undermine the bargaining process. 
 
Negotiating Team Responsibilities 
 
Attorney Upton explained that Board members do not currently serve on the District's negotiating 
teams.  He indicated that this arrangement helps avoid situations in which Board members become 
directly involved in negotiating individual contract provisions and are subsequently required to vote 
on those agreements. 
 
Attorney Upton explained that negotiating team members who support a tentative agreement are 
generally expected to continue supporting it during ratification. He described a limited exception in 
which a team member may reserve the right to oppose a particular provision by expressly declining 
to support it during negotiations.
October 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 9 of 13 
 
Committee Questions and Responses 
Committee Member Turner —   
1. She asked whether the categories of prohibited bargaining subjects were unique to New 
Hampshire or generally consistent throughout the country. 
 
Attorney Upton explained that the examples presented were based on New Hampshire case law but 
were generally consistent with practices throughout much of the northeastern United States. 
He noted that Maine has a more developed body of case law regarding mandatory, permissive, and 
prohibited bargaining subjects. He explained that New Hampshire's legal standards continue to 
evolve as additional cases are decided.  He reiterated the importance of carefully evaluating whether 
the District should voluntarily negotiate matters that could otherwise remain within its authority. 
 
2. Committee Member Turner asked what process applies when one party believes the other is 
not bargaining in good faith and whether the matter would proceed to mediation. 
 
Attorney Upton explained that allegations of unfair labor practices may be filed with the New 
Hampshire Public Employee Labor Relations Board.  He noted that the PELRB may determine that a 
party has failed to negotiate in good faith and direct that party to resume negotiations appropriately. 
However, Attorney Upton explained that such proceedings can be expensive and may create 
additional tension between the parties.  He stated that he generally prefers attempting to address 
concerns directly with the other party's representative before pursuing a formal complaint. 
If those efforts are unsuccessful, mediation may provide a more productive alternative because the 
mediator can work with both negotiating teams to identify obstacles and facilitate further discussion. 
 
3. Committee Member Turner asked what happens when the parties are unable to reach a new 
agreement after an existing contract expires. She questioned whether the current agreement 
simply continues for another year. 
 
Attorney Upton explained that New Hampshire law generally requires the parties to maintain the 
status quo regarding existing terms and conditions of employment.  He stated that certain provisions 
of the expired agreement continue while negotiations remain unresolved. 
General salary increases are typically not implemented during the status quo period, although certain 
exceptions may apply.
October 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 10 of 13 
 
 
Attorney Upton discussed quid pro quo benefits and provided the example of an employee who 
obtains a master's degree and qualifies for a contractual salary track change.  He explained that the 
employee may remain entitled to that adjustment because the educational requirement was completed 
in reliance upon the established compensation structure. Other terms and conditions, including health 
insurance provisions and employee contribution requirements, generally remain unchanged until a 
new agreement is reached. 
 
4. Committee Member Turner asked whether the cost of mediation was comparable to the cost 
of arbitration or fact-finding. 
 
Attorney Upton explained that mediators are generally compensated through a daily fee. 
Mediation typically does not involve the preparation of a formal written decision.  By contrast, 
arbitration and fact-finding proceedings often involve hearing time and additional expenses 
associated with preparing written findings, recommendations, or decisions.  Attorney Upton noted 
that complex mediation matters may require multiple sessions.  He referenced a current mediation 
involving a federal mediation service based in Boston but did not discuss the specific negotiations. 
 
Committee Member Want —  
 
1. Committee Member Want asked whether Attorney Upton, as the District's lead negotiator, 
was also required to support the agreements he negotiated when presenting them to the Board. 
 
Attorney Upton confirmed that he was the lead negotiator.  He explained that he would not agree to a 
provision that he or the negotiating team was unwilling to recommend to the Board.  If the 
negotiating team had significant concerns about a union proposal, Attorney Upton stated that he 
would seek input from the Board before agreeing to it.  He emphasized that the objective was to 
negotiate an agreement capable of receiving the required approvals rather than present an agreement 
that was unlikely to be ratified. 
 
2. Committee Member Want asked how Board members could provide input regarding their 
contractual priorities before negotiations begin and expressed concern that the Board may not 
have sufficient opportunity to communicate desired changes before the negotiating team
October 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 11 of 13 
 
reaches a tentative agreement.  Committee Member Want noted that rejecting an agreement at 
the end of the process could result in significant additional work after substantial time and 
effort had already been invested. 
 
Attorney Upton explained that the negotiating team identifies potential contract changes through 
consultation with District administrators, principals, and other staff familiar with the operational 
impact of existing provisions.  He stated that the team evaluates and prioritizes proposed changes 
based on their importance to District operations. 
 
Attorney Upton acknowledged that Board members may have additional priorities and indicated that 
opportunities could be established during upcoming meetings for members to identify issues they 
would like addressed.  He emphasized that, because negotiations involve compromise, the 
negotiating team may not be able to accomplish every requested change. 
 
Attorney Upton also explained that the Board retains the authority to reject a tentative agreement if 
members believe it does not adequately meet the District's needs. 
 
3. Committee Member Want noted that union membership follows a similar ratification process. 
The union negotiating team presents a tentative agreement to its members, who may approve 
or reject it. 
 
Attorney Upton acknowledged the comparison and explained that the District has previously received 
Board feedback regarding specific contractual provisions during confidential discussions.  He 
provided hypothetical examples of issues Board members might ask the negotiating team to address, 
including: 
 Increasing opportunities for parent-teacher conferences. 
 Improving parent access to teachers outside regular instructional hours. 
 Addressing contractual provisions that affect school operations or generate constituent 
concerns. 
Attorney Upton indicated that more specific examples involving current negotiations could be 
discussed separately following the public meeting.
October 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 12 of 13 
 
Vice Chair O'Connell —  
1. Vice Chair O'Connell asked how many collective bargaining agreements were currently 
involved in the District's negotiation cycle and requested that Attorney Upton identify the 
bargaining units. 
 
Attorney Upton initially estimated that approximately seven contracts were involved. During the 
discussion, the following six bargaining groups were identified: 
1. Principals. 
2. Manchester Educational Support Personnel Association (MESPA). 
3. Paraprofessionals. 
4. Teachers. 
5. Nurses. 
6. Amalgamated Transit Union (ATU). 
 
AFSCME was also referenced in connection with the paraprofessional bargaining unit. 
Attorney Upton subsequently indicated that the total appeared to be six bargaining groups. 
 
2. Vice Chair O'Connell asked whether the District utilizes one negotiating team for all 
bargaining units or establishes separate teams for each agreement.  He also asked who 
determines the composition of the negotiating teams. 
 
Attorney Upton explained that the composition of the negotiating teams varies depending upon the 
bargaining unit involved.  He noted that negotiations had not yet begun for several units and that the 
teams for those negotiations had not been finalized. 
 
Attorney Upton explained that a typical District negotiating team includes: 
 Superintendent Dr. Chmiel. 
 Attorney Matthew Upton. 
 Human Resources representative Michelle Evans. 
 An assistant superintendent whose responsibilities involve the employees covered by the 
agreement.
October 28, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 13 of 13 
 
Additional personnel may be consulted based on their knowledge and expertise.  For example, 
negotiations involving nurses may include input from nursing supervisors and District staff 
responsible for nursing operations. 
 
Attorney Upton emphasized that the team seeks to include individuals who understand the 
operational responsibilities and needs associated with each bargaining unit. 
 
3. Vice Chair O'Connell expressed support for the District's current practice of not including 
Board members directly on negotiating teams.  He recalled concerns associated with previous 
arrangements and indicated that he believed the current structure was more appropriate. 
 
4. Vice Chair O'Connell asked whether the Board could adjourn the public meeting and continue 
discussing current bargaining matters with Attorney Upton. 
 
Attorney Upton confirmed that discussions involving current negotiations and bargaining strategy 
could occur separately under the applicable provisions of New Hampshire law.  He indicated that 
several specific circumstances associated with ongoing negotiations warranted additional Board 
awareness and agreed to remain available following the meeting.  No specific negotiating strategies 
or confidential bargaining positions were discussed during the public portion of the meeting. 
 
 ADJOURNMENT 
 
6. This being a special meeting of the board, no further business can be presented unless by 2/3 
majority and a motion is in order to adjourn. 
 
 
This being a special meeting no further business was discussed.  On motion of Committee 
Member O’Connell, duly seconded by Committee Member Turner, it was moved to adjourn.  All 
were in favor, meeting adjourned at 6:46 p.m.
